title: Soccer, Nails, and Dreams: The Women of the World Cup
summary: Have you ever seen soccer-themed nail art? At the 2026 World Cup, reporter Jasmine Garsd noticed something cool: many women had tiny flags, trophies, and soccer balls painted on their nails! She visited nail salons in Houston, Texas, where customers talked about their favorite players while getting designs that took hours to create. But the best part of her journey was meeting women who love soccer deeply. One was 22-year-old Zhraa Hamidy. She fell in love with soccer as a kid and even got a college scholarship for it. But her father said soccer wasn't for women, so she couldn't take it. Now, she coaches a girls' team in Michigan called Michigan FC. Most of the players are young Muslim women. One star player, 16-year-old Fatima Alzahraa Yazdchi, amazed everyone with her dribbling skills. She wants to earn a soccer scholarship for college. When asked about her favorite goal ever, she didn't pick a famous player's goal—she picked her own! She described kicking the ball from 40 yards out, right over the goalie's hands. Jasmine understands these feelings. She grew up in Argentina, where soccer is a huge deal. She played with boys in her neighborhood, but her own father also told her soccer wasn't for girls. She felt crushed. But she found a way back to the sport by writing about it. Now, she sees the same joy in girls like Fatima. The World Cup might be full of cheering crowds, but the real magic happens on small fields where girls dare to dream big.
why_it_matters: This story shows that no matter who you are, you can follow your passion for a sport, and by playing together, girls can change old rules about what they're 'supposed' to do.

background_read: The Women's World Cup is a huge international soccer tournament held every four years, just like the men's one, but women's soccer has only recently gotten as much attention.
In many cultures and families, girls have been discouraged from playing soccer because of old-fashioned ideas about what girls should do.
The 2026 World Cup meant millions of fans celebrated soccer, but for girls like Fatima, the real victory is being allowed to play and dream.
Article_Structure: WHO: Young women like Zhraa Hamidy, Fatima Alzahraa Yazdchi, and reporter Jasmine Garsd, who love soccer.
WHAT: They overcome family doubts about girls playing soccer, showing their skills—from nail art at the World Cup to Fatima's amazing 40-yard goal.
WHERE: In Houston, Texas, at the World Cup; in Michigan at a girls' soccer club; and in Argentina where Jasmine grew up.
WHY: Because the joy of soccer is powerful, and they want to inspire more girls to dream big and earn college scholarships.

perspectives.description: She feels unstoppable when she plays, proud of her own amazing goals, and dreams of going to college on a soccer scholarship.
He believes soccer is not for women, perhaps because of cultural norms, and stops his daughter from playing, not realizing how much it means to her.
She knows the pain of being told 'no' but found another way to stay close to soccer by writing about it, and now she finds hope in seeing girls like Fatima succeed.
